Chapter 6: Regret and the Choices We Make.
Every day, we're faced with choices—some are tiny, barely a blip on our radar, while others feel like they could change everything. And let’s be honest, regret often lingers in the background, especially when the stakes are high or the outcome’s uncertain.
But have you ever wondered if regret could actually help you make better decisions in the future?
Imagine a young professional, right at a crossroads. She’s got two job offers. One promises stability, the other promises adventure. She goes back and forth, replaying all the possible futures in her mind. The fear of future regret? It’s almost overwhelming. What if she picks the wrong one? The funny thing is, most of us don’t even notice how much the anticipation of regret influences us. Sometimes, it pushes us toward the choice that feels true to who we are. Other times, it leaves us stuck, unable to choose at all.
Here’s something interesting: the author points out that, in those big moments, we often imagine our future selves looking back on this exact decision. It’s like a little bit of mental time travel. This can really help us figure out what matters most. But it can also make us second-guess ourselves endlessly.
Take the story of a father, for example. He moves his family to a new city and spends countless nights worrying—did he just uproot his children for nothing? Did he make a huge mistake leaving behind everything familiar? Even years later, he sometimes wonders if he chose right. But then, he sees his kids thriving in their new home, and that regret starts to fade. Suddenly, it’s clear—most choices aren’t as final as we think. Life gives us room to adjust, to learn, and to grow.
So, regret isn’t just about looking back. It’s woven into the decisions we make every day. It can sharpen our focus, help us see what’s truly important, and even keep us from repeating mistakes. But if we’re not careful, it can also trap us in endless loops of “what if,” especially when we convince ourselves there’s only one right answer.
There’s also the story of a woman who, after a painful breakup, finds herself unable to commit to anyone new. She’s terrified she’ll make the same mistake and feel that old regret all over again. It’s only when she realizes that regret is part of loving deeply—that it means she cared—that she finally lets herself move forward.
Most people don’t realize this, but regret is actually a sign that you’re paying attention. It means you care about the outcome. It’s a reminder that our choices matter—but also, that no choice is ever perfect. The real wisdom? It’s learning to live with imperfection, making decisions bravely, and trusting that even our regrets can help us grow.
